title: Volume of 1 M H2SO4 needed for the ammonia from a Kjeldahl estimation
summary: Build the compound before you analyse it. The bench walks the printed reaction sequence in three stages - J, then K weighed against the stem's own 350 g/mol checksum, then L - and then stops and makes you commit: L carries two nitrogen atoms, so how many moles of ammonia come off per mole of L? The clock waits for your answer. Only then does it digest, distil and titrate, and the titre it reports is the one your commitment earns.
subject: Chemistry
chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
topic: Kjeldahl estimation of nitrogen, on a compound built by a reaction sequence
subtopics: Friedel-Crafts acylation and where two methyl groups send the acyl
The Finkelstein exchange, and why the iodide is made first
Williamson ether synthesis from a phenoxide
Selective reduction: NaBH4 takes the ketone and leaves the nitro group
Molar mass assembled atom by atom from given atomic masses
Using a stated molar mass as a checksum on a proposed structure
The Kjeldahl method and the nitrogens it cannot estimate
Acid-base stoichiometry with a dibasic acid
Molarity to volume, and answering in the unit asked for
concepts: The stem prints one molar mass, 350 for K, and that number is a checksum rather than decoration: whatever structure is proposed for K has to weigh exactly 350 on the given atomic masses, which confirms the whole sequence before any arithmetic begins
m-Xylene's two methyl groups are both o,p-directing, so the acyl group enters the one ring position activated by both of them
The chloride is exchanged for iodide before the phenoxide step because iodide is the better leaving group - the Finkelstein exchange is there to serve the substitution that follows

Sodium borohydride is chosen for its selectivity: it reduces the ketone to a secondary alcohol and leaves the aromatic nitro group completely untouched, which is exactly why the nitro group survives all the way to L
L contains TWO nitrogen atoms - one amine and one nitro - and the entire question turns on that fact being noticed
Kjeldahl's digestion converts nitrogen to ammonium only from amine-like nitrogen; nitro, azo, diazo and ring nitrogen are not reduced and are never estimated, so only one of L's two nitrogens is seen
The method therefore under-reports a nitro compound: it finds about 4.9 per cent nitrogen in L where 9.8 per cent is actually present, and the gap is the nitro nitrogen
Sulphuric acid is dibasic: 2 NH3 + H2SO4 gives (NH4)2SO4, so the moles of acid are half the moles of ammonia - a factor that is trivial to state and easy to drop
Molarity is moles per litre, so dividing moles by molarity gives litres and the thousand has to be put back to answer in millilitres

Stopping the sequence one step early, at J with 285, gives 10.04 mL - so close to the right answer that it cannot be caught by a plausibility check, which is why the structure has to be tracked properly
Of the seven atomic masses printed in the stem, S and Ba belong to Q.18 and never enter this answer, while Br enters only to verify the 350
formulas: M = sum of (atom count x atomic mass), built from the stem's own values
n(NH3) = n(L) x (nitrogens DIGESTED, not nitrogens present)
% N estimated = 1400 x n(NH3)/w(L);  % N present = 1400 x 2 n(L)/w(L)

methods: Derived from first principles before any published solution was consulted: the reaction sequence, every structure, both molar masses and the Kjeldahl limitation were each fixed independently, and only then was the answer compared with an external source

Every molar mass in the simulation is assembled atom by atom from the atomic masses printed in the stem rather than taken from a table, so the page recomputes them live if any of those masses is edited

The question's own internal checksum satisfied exactly: the independently constructed K = C16H16BrNO3 comes to 192 + 16 + 80 + 14 + 48 = 350 g/mol, precisely the molar mass the stem states, which confirms the whole assignment rather than assuming it

Three separate masses in one stem all resolve to round amounts, which corroborates the structures further: 5.72 g of L is exactly 0.02 mol on M(L) = 286, 3.79 g of M is exactly 0.01 mol on M(M) = 379, and that in turn gives exactly 2.33 g of BaSO4 for Q.18

The crux identified as a syllabus limitation rather than an arithmetic step: Kjeldahl digestion reduces amine-type nitrogen to ammonium but not nitro, azo, diazo or ring nitrogen, so exactly one of L's two nitrogens is estimated. This single decision separates 10 mL from 20 mL and the page makes the student commit to it before the titration runs

The under-reporting made quantitative as a consistency check: the method finds 4.90 per cent nitrogen in L while 9.79 per cent is actually present, and the ratio of those two figures is exactly 1:2, as it must be for one of two nitrogens
The stoichiometry checked in both directions: 2 NH3 + H2SO4 -> (NH4)2SO4 gives n(acid) = n(NH3)/2, and the dimensional chain mol / (mol/L) = L, x1000 = mL confirms the unit asked for

The model checked away from the paper's numbers, and the simulation reproduces each case live: 11.44 g of L requires 20 mL, so the titre is linear in the mass; 2 M acid requires 5 mL, so it is inverse in the strength; and changing the atomic masses of S and Ba leaves the answer at 10 mL, which is the structural reason those two belong to Q.18

The broken-checksum case handled as a note rather than a refusal: entering the atomic mass of carbon as 13 makes K weigh 366 and the bench says so on the rail, while still running - the checksum is the student's evidence, not a gate on the experiment

The distractors reproduced deliberately, each as a run of the model with one wrong assumption on the student's own data: counting both nitrogens gives 20 mL, treating H2SO4 as monobasic gives 20 mL, both mistakes together give 40 mL, using the stem's 350 in place of M(L) gives 8.17 mL, stopping at J with 285 gives 10.04 mL, and answering in litres gives 0.01. None is 10 by a correct route, and the 10.04 near-miss is called out on the page as the dangerous one because no plausibility check can catch it
Independent numeric script with every formula assembled atom by atom (verify17.py): 23 of 23 checks pass and the answer is 10 mL

Headless-browser run of the finished page: 113 assertions driving the whole flow - the structures and the checksum, the model's behaviour away from the paper's numbers, the reaction scheme confirmed to be live SVG rather than an image with all three reagent steps named, the empty rail with the answer nowhere on it, the checksum note appearing and clearing, rejection of unreadable input, each of the five stages in turn with its reasoning and its arithmetic written in the student's own numbers, the prediction gate confirmed to hold the clock at t = 2.3 s and to accept a wrong commitment rather than blocking it, a fourteen-frame leak sweep confirming the answer appears on no stage before the reveal, the blackout then flash then graffiti reveal with its particle burst, the header blinking once and stopping, the nitrogen-audit cards, both chart views, the explorer confirmed to double the titre at 11.44 g, three runs on different data, all six traps, classroom mode with NEXT STEP walking the beats one press at a time and the gate holding it too, replay clearing the earlier prediction, speed, theme toggle, a deck that fits in one window at 621 px, unique ids, accessible labels, a clean console and zero horizontal overflow at 390 px and 360 px
A separate reduced-motion run confirmed the blink, the reveal flash and the card animations are all suppressed while the content and the answer remain complete

Answer cross-checked afterwards against a published worked solution for this paper, which reports the same M(L) = 286, states explicitly that one mole of L releases one mole of ammonia because the nitro nitrogen is not estimated, and gives the same answer, 10 mL. verification.note: Q.17 and Q.18 share one question stem in Section 4. This simulation answers Q.17; the page builds M as far as identifying it and then leaves Q.18's Carius calculation alone, so the two halves do not give each other away. Section 4 is marked +2 for the correct value and 0 otherwise. The reaction scheme is redrawn as live vector structures rather than reproduced from the exam PDF, so the paper itself is never published. Revision 2 rebuilt the page against a second, much longer specification for the same question: it adds the m-xylene opening scene, the reagent shelf, a branching stage at K with both products drawn, five further prediction gates, IUPAC name badges, the ammonia collection meter and the burette delivery. The chemistry, the answer and the simulation ID are unchanged.

interactivity: Build the compound, commit at every turn, then run the analysis: the bench takes the printed sequence apart in six stages and produces the titre at the end - about a minute end to end, longer with a class
The experiment happens inside a dark laboratory chamber that stays dark in either page theme, while the page around it follows the light or dark theme like every other simulation in the library
It opens on m-xylene itself, named as the starting material, with C8H10 and 8 C + 10 H = 106 g/mol summed from the atomic masses in the rail - nothing is asserted that the page has not just computed

A reagent shelf of eight bottles sits under the bench: ClCH2COCl, AlCl3, NaI, the nitrophenoxide, NaBH4, PBr3, ammonia and PhSNa. The bottle in use lights up as the synthesis runs, and tapping any of them says what it is for and why it was chosen

SIX prediction gates, one per stage, and each one stops the clock until the student commits: what the ring does to chloroacetyl chloride, what NaBH4 reduces when a ketone and a nitro group are both present, which of the two routes out of K this question needs, what excess ammonia gives with a benzylic bromide, how many of L's two nitrogens Kjeldahl can see, and how many moles of acid neutralise the ammonia
A wrong commitment is accepted and marked, never blocked - the point is to have an opinion on record before the bench settles it, and no option text carries the answer

The printed reaction scheme is redrawn on the page as live vector structures - four benzene rings, real bonds, every reagent named - so the exam PDF is never published and the structures can be read at any zoom

Nine inputs with a typed box, a slider and a pair of large steppers each: the mass of L, the strength of the acid and the seven atomic masses, so every molar mass on the page is recomputed from what is entered rather than hard-coded
Eight live instruments that stay blank until the run establishes them - M(J), M(K), M(L), n(L), the nitrogen count, the ammonia, the acid and finally the titre, which stays blank until the very end

Stage 01 builds J and explains where the acyl group lands and why the iodide is made before the phenoxide step, then assembles M(J) = 285 atom by atom from the entered masses. J is named in full underneath

Stage 02 is the checksum: NaBH4 reduces the ketone while the nitro group is left alone, PBr3 puts the bromine in, and K is weighed on a live balance against the stem's stated 350 with the sum written out term by term. If the entered atomic masses no longer reproduce 350 the rail says so, but the experiment still runs, because the checksum is evidence and not a gate

Stage 03 is a branching synthesis tree: K sits at the left with two glowing routes leaving it - excess ammonia to L, the nitrogen compound, and PhSNa to M, the sulphur compound. Both are drawn, named and weighed once a route is taken, and choosing the sulphur route is answered honestly rather than refused: that is Q.18's compound, so the bench says so and follows L
Stage 04 builds L, states in one line that it now contains TWO nitrogen atoms, and works out 5.72 / 286 = 0.02 mol

Stage 05 stops the experiment: both nitrogens are circled on the molecule and the student has to commit to how many moles of ammonia come off per mole of L before the audit resolves the amine nitrogen as counted and the nitro nitrogen as surviving the digestion

Stage 06 runs the method in three cards: the digestion flask over a flame with ammonium building up, the distillation carrying the ammonia into the standard acid past a collection meter that fills to 0.02 mol, and the titration arithmetic with the burette delivering while its reading stays withheld

The burette reading is withheld until the answer is revealed, and only then does returning to stage 06 show it stopping at the titre it actually took - the standing rule that the answer stays hidden until the experiment concludes outranks showing the delivery early

The reveal darkens the laboratory for about a second, then flashes, sprays the answer across the chamber in graffiti lettering with a burst of confetti and chemical glyphs, blinks the header answer box once and unlocks the derivation

A permanent nitrogen audit below the bench sets what the method reports against what the molecule actually contains - 4.90 per cent against 9.79 per cent - so the under-reporting is a number rather than a claim
A titre-against-mass line drawn from the entered data with a slider to explore any sample mass, and a second view contrasting one nitrogen estimated against two counted
A record of the run that fills in quantity by quantity, a trial log of every completed run, and an insight card naming what can and cannot move the answer

Six cards on the mistakes this question really produces, each re-running the model with one wrong assumption on the student's own numbers: 20, 20, 40, 8.17, 10.04 and 0.01 - including the 285 near-miss that no plausibility check can catch

CLASSROOM MODE for a projector: the rail, the shelf and the surrounding sections are hidden, the stage and the narration scale up, and NEXT STEP walks the class through the whole sequence one press at a time - and every one of the six gates holds NEXT STEP too, so the class has to answer before the teacher can move on

A full-screen button for the bench, playback controls - pause, resume, replay, 0.5x / 1x / 2x - and a change-the-data button that returns to the rail with the entries kept; replay clears every prediction so all six gates are live again
Step-by-step solution with an independent verification log, gated until the answer is revealed
Four concept cards - the reaction sequence, the 350 checksum, which nitrogens Kjeldahl can see, and the dibasic acid - that animate in when the answer lands and fill their numbers in only then
